# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html

# tempfile/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! - Use [`tempfile()`] when you need a real [`std::fs::File`] but don't need to refer to it
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!   by-path.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! - Use [`NamedTempFile::new()`] when you need a _named_ temporary file that can be referred to its
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!   path.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - Use [`tempdir()`] when you need a temporary directory that will be recursively deleted on drop.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - Use [`spooled_tempfile()`] when you need an in-memory buffer that will ultimately be backed by
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   a temporary file if it gets too large.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! # Design
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! [`tempfile()`] relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [`TempDir`] and [`NamedTempFile`] both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ## Resource Leaking
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! `tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! `NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don't run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [`lazy_static`]), among other possible reasons.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! ## Unexpected File Deletion
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven't been accessed recently
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! (often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! [temporary file cleaner](#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ## Security
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! temporary directories by default. Importantly, it's not relevant for Windows or macOS as both
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [`env::override_temp_dir`] to
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! directory ([`env::temp_dir`]) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! temporary file cleaner, etc.).
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ### Temporary File Cleaners
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! This isn't an issue for [`tempfile`] as it doesn't rely on file paths. However, [`NamedTempFile`]
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! and temporary directories _do_ rely on file paths for _some_ operations. See the security
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! documentation on the [`NamedTempFile`] and the [`TempDir`] types for more information.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! Mitigation:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! - This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!   temporary files that haven't been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! - Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!   cleaners.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ### Access Permissions
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! Temporary _files_ created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! However, temporary _directories_ are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! directory.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! ### Denial of Service
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! If the file-name randomness ([`Builder::rand_bytes`]) is too small and/or this crate is built
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! without the `getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service

[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!    of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger

[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!    create temporary a file (when the `getrandom` feature is enabled as it is by default on all
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!    major platforms).
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!

[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!

[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! ```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! ```
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! use tempfile::tempdir;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! use std::fs::File;
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! use std::io::Write;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! // Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! let dir = tempdir()?;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! // By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! // been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! // the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! // of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! // succeeded.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! drop(file);
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! dir.close()?;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! ```
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! [`tempfile()`]: fn.tempfile.html
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! [`tempdir()`]: fn.tempdir.html
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! [`TempDir`]: struct.TempDir.html
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! [`NamedTempFile`]: struct.NamedTempFile.html
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! [`lazy_static`]: https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62

[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// Create a new `Builder`.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// # Examples
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    ///
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// Create a named temporary file and write some data into it:
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    ///
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// use std::ffi::OsStr;
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    ///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ///     .prefix("my-temporary-note")
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///     .suffix(".txt")
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    ///     .rand_bytes(5)
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///     .tempfile()?;
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// let name = named_tempfile
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///     .path()
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///     .file_name().and_then(OsStr::to_str);
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// if let Some(name) = name {
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///     assert!(name.starts_with("my-temporary-note"));
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///     assert!(name.ends_with(".txt"));
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///     assert_eq!(name.len(), "my-temporary-note.txt".len() + 5);
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// ```
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// ```
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// use std::io::Write;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// use std::fs::File;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// use std::ffi::OsStr;
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// let dir = Builder::new()
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///     .prefix("my-temporary-dir")
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///     .rand_bytes(5)
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///     .tempdir()?;
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// // By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// // been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// // the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// // of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// // succeeded.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// drop(file);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// dir.close()?;
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// ```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    ///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// Create a temporary directory with a chosen prefix under a chosen folder:
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// ```no_run
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    ///

[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// ```

[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// Set the permissions for the new temporary file/directory.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    ///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// # Platform Notes
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    ///
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// ## Windows
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// This setting is only fully-supported on unix-like platforms. On Windows, if this method is
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// called with a [`Permissions`] object where `permissions.readonly` returns true, creating
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// temporary files and directories will fail with an error.
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// ## Unix
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// On unix-like systems, the actual permission bits set on the tempfile or tempdir will be
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// affected by the `umask` applied by the underlying syscall. The actual permission bits are
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// calculated via `permissions & !umask`. In other words, depending on your umask, the
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// permissions of the created file may be more restrictive (but never more permissive) than the
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// ones you specified.
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    ///
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// Permissions default to `0o600` for tempfiles and `0o777` for tempdirs. Note, this doesn't
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// include effects of the current `umask`. For example, combined with the standard umask
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// `0o022`, the defaults yield `0o600` for tempfiles and `0o755` for tempdirs.
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    ///
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// ## WASI
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    ///
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// While custom permissions are allowed on WASI, they will be ignored as the platform has no
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// concept of permissions or file modes (or multiple users for that matter).
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// # Examples
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// Create a named temporary file that is world-readable.
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// ```
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// # #[cfg(unix)]
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// # {
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// let all_read_write = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o666);
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// let tempfile = Builder::new().permissions(all_read_write).tempfile()?;
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    ///
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// // Check that this worked and that the file is world-readable.
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// //
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// // NOTE: the file likely won't actually be created with 0o666 permissions because it's
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// // restricted by the user's umask.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// //
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// // NOTE: This test will fail if the user's umask is, e.g., 0o066.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// let actual_permissions = tempfile.path().metadata()?.permissions();
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// assert_eq!(actual_permissions.mode() & 0o044, 0o044);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// # }
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// ```
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    ///
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// Create a named temporary directory that is restricted to the owner.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    ///
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    /// ```
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// # #[cfg(unix)]
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// # {
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// let owner_rwx = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o700);
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// let tempdir = Builder::new().permissions(owner_rwx).tempdir()?;
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// let actual_permissions = tempdir.path().metadata()?.permissions();
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// assert_eq!(
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///     actual_permissions.mode() & !0o170000,
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    ///     0o700,
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///     "we get the narrow permissions we asked for"
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// );
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// # }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// ```
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    pub fn permissions(&mut self, permissions: [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html)) -> &mut Self {
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        [self](https://docs.rs#460).permissions = [Some](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)([permissions](https://docs.rs#460));
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        [self](https://docs.rs#460)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    }
[464](https://docs.rs#464)
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// Disable cleanup of the file/folder to even when the [`NamedTempFile`]/[`TempDir`] goes out
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// of scope. Prefer [`NamedTempFile::keep`] and [`TempDir::keep`] where possible;
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// `disable_cleanup` is provided for testing & debugging.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    ///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// By default, the file/folder is automatically cleaned up in the destructor of
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// [`NamedTempFile`]/[`TempDir`]. When `disable_cleanup` is set to `true`, this behavior is
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// suppressed. If you wish to disable cleanup after creating a temporary file/directory, call
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    /// [`NamedTempFile::disable_cleanup`] or [`TempDir::disable_cleanup`].
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    ///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// # Warnings
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    ///
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// On some platforms (for now, only Windows), temporary files are marked with a special
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    /// "temporary file" (`FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY`) attribute. Disabling cleanup _will not_ unset
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    /// this attribute while calling [`NamedTempFile::keep`] will.
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    ///
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    /// # Examples
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    ///
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    /// ```
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    ///
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    /// let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    ///     .disable_cleanup(true)
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    ///     .tempfile()?;
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// ```
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    pub fn disable_cleanup(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self {
[491](https://docs.rs#491)        [self](https://docs.rs#490).disable_cleanup = [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#490);
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        [self](https://docs.rs#490)
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    }
[494](https://docs.rs#494)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// Deprecated alias for [`Builder::disable_cleanup`].
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    #[deprecated = "Use Builder::disable_cleanup"]
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    pub fn keep(&mut self, keep: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self {
[498](https://docs.rs#498)        [self](https://docs.rs#497).[disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#490-493)([keep](https://docs.rs#497))
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    }

[630](https://docs.rs#630)
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    /// Attempts to create a temporary file (or file-like object) using the
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    /// provided closure. The closure is passed a temporary file path and
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// returns an [`std::io::Result`]. The path provided to the closure will be
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    /// inside of [`env::temp_dir()`]. Use [`Builder::make_in`] to provide
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// a custom temporary directory. If the closure returns one of the
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// following errors, then another randomized file path is tried:
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    ///  - [`std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists`]
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    ///  - [`std::io::ErrorKind::AddrInUse`]
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    ///
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// This can be helpful for taking full control over the file creation, but
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// leaving the temporary file path construction up to the library. This
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// also enables creating a temporary UNIX domain socket, since it is not
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// possible to bind to a socket that already exists.
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// Note that [`Builder::append`] is ignored when using [`Builder::make`].
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    ///
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// # Security
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    ///
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// This has the same [security implications][security] as
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// [`NamedTempFile`], but with additional caveats. Specifically, it is up
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    /// to the closure to ensure that the file does not exist and that such a
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    /// check is *atomic*. Otherwise, a [time-of-check to time-of-use
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// bug][TOCTOU] could be introduced.
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    ///
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// For example, the following is **not** secure:
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    ///
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    /// ```
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// use std::fs::File;
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    ///
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// // This is NOT secure!
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| {
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    ///     if path.is_file() {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    ///         return Err(std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists.into());
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    ///     }
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    ///
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    ///     // Between the check above and the usage below, an attacker could
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///     // have replaced `path` with another file, which would get truncated
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    ///     // by `File::create`.
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    ///
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    ///     File::create(path)
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// })?;
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// ```
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    ///
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// Note that simply using [`std::fs::File::create`] alone is not correct
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    /// because it does not fail if the file already exists:
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    ///
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    /// ```
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// use std::fs::File;
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    ///
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// // This could overwrite an existing file!
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| File::create(path))?;
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// ```
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    /// For creating regular temporary files, use [`Builder::tempfile`] instead
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// to avoid these problems. This function is meant to enable more exotic
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// use-cases.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    ///
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    /// # Resource leaking
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    ///
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// See [the resource leaking][resource-leaking] docs on `NamedTempFile`.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    ///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// # Errors
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    ///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// If the closure returns any error besides
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// [`std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists`] or
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// [`std::io::ErrorKind::AddrInUse`], then `Err` is returned.
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    ///
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// # Examples
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// ```
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    /// # #[cfg(unix)]
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    /// # {
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    /// use std::os::unix::net::UnixListener;
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    ///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// let tempsock = Builder::new().make(|path| UnixListener::bind(path))?;
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    /// # }
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    /// ```
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    ///
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    /// [TOCTOU]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-of-check_to_time-of-use
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    /// [security]: struct.NamedTempFile.html#security
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    /// [resource-leaking]: struct.NamedTempFile.html#resource-leaking
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    pub fn make<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> io::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#497-500)<R>>
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    where
[718](https://docs.rs#718)        F: [FnMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnMut.html)(&[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)) -> io::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<R>,
[719](https://docs.rs#719)    {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        [self](https://docs.rs#716).[make_in](https://docs.rs#739-756)(env::[temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env.rs.html#45-51)(), [f](https://docs.rs#716))
[721](https://docs.rs#721)    }
[722](https://docs.rs#722)
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    /// This is the same as [`Builder::make`], except `dir` is used as the base
[724](https://docs.rs#724)    /// directory for the temporary file path.
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    ///
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    /// See [`Builder::make`] for more details and security implications.
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    ///
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    /// # Examples
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    /// ```
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    /// # #[cfg(unix)]
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    /// # {
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    /// use tempfile::Builder;
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// use std::os::unix::net::UnixListener;
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    ///
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// let tempsock = Builder::new().make_in("./", |path| UnixListener::bind(path))?;
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// # }
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// # Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    /// ```
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    pub fn make_in<F, R, P>(&self, dir: P, mut f: F) -> io::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#497-500)<R>>
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    where
[741](https://docs.rs#741)        F: [FnMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnMut.html)(&[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)) -> io::[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<R>,
[742](https://docs.rs#742)        P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>,
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    {
[744](https://docs.rs#744)        util::[create_helper](https://docs.rs/util.rs.html#22-82)(
[745](https://docs.rs#745)            [dir](https://docs.rs#739).[as_ref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html#tymethod.as_ref)(),
[746](https://docs.rs#746)            [self](https://docs.rs#739).prefix,
[747](https://docs.rs#747)            [self](https://docs.rs#739).suffix,
[748](https://docs.rs#748)            [self](https://docs.rs#739).random_len,
[749](https://docs.rs#749)            move |path| {
[750](https://docs.rs#750)                [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)([NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#497-500)::[from_parts](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#918-920)(
[751](https://docs.rs#751)                    f(&path)?,
[752](https://docs.rs#752)                    [TempPath](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#130-133)::[new](https://docs.rs/file/mod.rs.html#388-393)([path](https://docs.rs#749), [self](https://docs.rs#739).disable_cleanup),
[753](https://docs.rs#753)                ))
[754](https://docs.rs#754)            },
[755](https://docs.rs#755)        )

# tempfile in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/fn.tempfile.html

## Expand description

Create a new temporary file. Also see [ tempfile_in](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile_in.html).

The file will be created in the location returned by [ env::temp_dir()](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This variant is secure/reliable in the presence of a pathological temporary file cleaner.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

The temporary file will be automatically removed by the OS when the last handle to it is closed. This doesn’t rely on Rust destructors being run, so will (almost) never fail to clean up the temporary file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

---

# NamedTempFile in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/struct.NamedTempFile.html

`pub struct NamedTempFile<F = `[File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A named temporary file.

The default constructor, [ NamedTempFile::new()](https://docs.rs#method.new), creates files in
the location returned by

[, but](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir()``NamedTempFile`
can be configured to manage a temporary file in any location
by constructing with [.](https://docs.rs#method.new_in)

`NamedTempFile::new_in()`[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Most operating systems employ temporary file cleaners to delete old
temporary files. Unfortunately these temporary file cleaners don’t always
reliably *detect* whether the temporary file is still being used.

Specifically, the following sequence of events can happen:

- A user creates a temporary file with `NamedTempFile::new()`.
- Time passes.
- The temporary file cleaner deletes (unlinks) the temporary file from the filesystem.
- Some other program creates a new file to replace this deleted temporary file.
- The user tries to re-open the temporary file (in the same program or in a different program) by path. Unfortunately, they’ll end up opening the file created by the other program, not the original file.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-system-specific-concerns)Operating System Specific Concerns

The behavior of temporary files and temporary file cleaners differ by operating system.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

On Windows, temporary files are, by default, created in per-user temporary
file directories so only an application running as the same user would be
able to interfere (which they could do anyways). However, an application
running as the same user can still *accidentally* re-create deleted
temporary files if the number of random bytes in the temporary file name is
too small.

[§](https://docs.rs#macos)MacOS

Like on Windows, temporary files are created in per-user temporary file
directories by default so calling `NamedTempFile::new()` should be
relatively safe.

[§](https://docs.rs#linux)Linux

Unfortunately, most *Linux* distributions don’t create per-user temporary
file directories. Worse, systemd’s tmpfiles daemon (a common temporary file
cleaner) will happily remove open temporary files if they haven’t been
modified within the last 10 days.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

If the program exits before the `NamedTempFile` destructor is
run, the temporary file will not be deleted. This can happen
if the process exits using [ std::process::exit()](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/fn.exit.html), a segfault occurs,
receiving an interrupt signal like

`SIGINT` that is not handled, or by using
a statically declared `NamedTempFile` instance (like with [).](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)

`lazy_static`Use the [ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) function unless you need a named file path.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#606-608)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#606-608)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)>

Create a new named temporary file.

See [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) for more configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-1)Security

This will create a temporary file in the default temporary file directory (platform dependent). This has security implications on many platforms so please read the security section of this type’s documentation.

Reasons to use this method:

-
The file has a short lifetime and your temporary file cleaner is sane (doesn’t delete recently accessed files).
-
You trust every user on your system (i.e. you are the only user).
-
You have disabled your system’s temporary file cleaner or verified that your system doesn’t have a temporary file cleaner.

Reasons not to use this method:

-
You’ll fix it later. No you won’t.
-
You don’t care about the security of the temporary file. If none of the “reasons to use this method” apply, referring to a temporary file by name may allow an attacker to create/overwrite your non-temporary files. There are exceptions but if you don’t already know them, don’t use this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a named temporary file and write some data to it:

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let mut file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NamedTempFile%3CF%3E)

### impl<F> [NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<F>

Get the temporary file’s path.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-2)Security

Referring to a temporary file’s path may not be secure in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
println!("{:?}", file.path());
```
Close and remove the temporary file.

Use this if you want to detect errors in deleting the file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

If the file cannot be deleted, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// By closing the `NamedTempFile` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the file will still be deleted when `file` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the file
// succeeded.
file.close()?;
```
Persist the temporary file at the target path.

If a file exists at the target path, persist will atomically replace it.
If this method fails, it will return `self` in the resulting
[ PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistError.html).

**Note:** Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems. Also
neither the file contents nor the containing directory are
synchronized, so the update may not yet have reached the disk when
`persist` returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-3)Security

This method persists the temporary file using its path and may not be secure in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
let mut persisted_file = file.persist("./saved_file.txt")?;
writeln!(persisted_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#821-833)#### pub fn [persist_noclobber](https://docs.rs#method.persist_noclobber)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(
    self,
    new_path: P,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<F, [PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistError.html)<F>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#821-833)

#### pub fn [persist_noclobber](https://docs.rs#method.persist_noclobber)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(
    self,
    new_path: P,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<F, [PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistError.html)<F>>

Persist the temporary file at the target path if and only if no file exists there.

If a file exists at the target path, fail. If this method fails, it will
return `self` in the resulting PersistError.

**Note:** Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems.

**Atomicity:** This method is not guaranteed to be atomic on all platforms, although it will
generally be atomic on Windows and modern Linux filesystems. While it will never overwrite a
file at the target path, it may leave the original link to the temporary file behind leaving
you with two [hard links](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_link) in your filesystem pointing at the same underlying file.
This can happen if either (a) we lack permission to “unlink” the original filename; (b) this
program crashes while persisting the temporary file; or (c) the filesystem is removed,
unmounted, etc. while we’re performing this operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-4)Security

This method persists the temporary file using its path and may not be secure in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location or a file already exists there,
`Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
let mut persisted_file = file.persist_noclobber("./saved_file.txt")?;
writeln!(persisted_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

#### pub fn [keep](https://docs.rs#method.keep)(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(F, [PathBuf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)), [PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistError.html)<F>>

Keep the temporary file from being deleted. This function will turn the temporary file into a non-temporary file without moving it.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-4)Errors

On some platforms (e.g., Windows), we need to mark the file as non-temporary. This operation could fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let mut file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let (file, path) = file.keep()?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#875-877)#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#875-877)

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Disable cleanup of the temporary file. If `disable_cleanup` is `true`, the temporary file
will not be deleted when this `TempPath` is dropped. This method is equivalent to calling
[ Builder::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.disable_cleanup) when creating the original

`NamedTempFile`, which see for
relevant warnings.**NOTE:** this method is primarily useful for testing/debugging. If you want to simply turn
a temporary file into a non-temporary file, prefer [ NamedTempFile::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#method.keep).

Turn this named temporary file into an “unnamed” temporary file as if you
had constructed it with [ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html).

The underlying file will be removed from the filesystem but the returned [ File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)
can still be read/written.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#902-904)#### pub fn [into_temp_path](https://docs.rs#method.into_temp_path)(self) -> [TempPath](https://docs.rs/struct.TempPath.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#902-904)

#### pub fn [into_temp_path](https://docs.rs#method.into_temp_path)(self) -> [TempPath](https://docs.rs/struct.TempPath.html)

Closes the file, leaving only the temporary file path.

This is useful when another process must be able to open the temporary file.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#923-955)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NamedTempFile-1)### impl [NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<[File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#923-955)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NamedTempFile-1)

### impl [NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<[File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)>

Securely reopen the temporary file.

This function is useful when you need multiple independent handles to
the same file. It’s perfectly fine to drop the original `NamedTempFile`
while holding on to `File`s returned by this function; the `File`s will
remain usable. However, they may not be nameable.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-5)Errors

If the file cannot be reopened, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-5)Security

Unlike `File::open(my_temp_file.path())`, `NamedTempFile::reopen()`
guarantees that the re-opened file is the *same* file, even in the
presence of pathological temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
let another_handle = file.reopen()?;
```

# tempdir in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/fn.tempdir.html

## Expand description

Create a new temporary directory. Also see [ tempdir_in](https://docs.rs/fn.tempdir_in.html).

The `tempdir` function creates a directory in the file system and returns a
[ TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html). The directory will be automatically deleted when the

`TempDir`’s
destructor is run.[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

See [the resource leaking](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#resource-leaking) docs on `TempDir`.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Temporary directories are created with the default permissions unless otherwise
specified via [ Builder::permissions](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.permissions). Depending on your platform, this may make
them world-readable.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`
let tmp_dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = tmp_dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut tmp_file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// `tmp_dir` goes out of scope, the directory as well as
// `tmp_file` will be deleted here.
drop(tmp_file);
tmp_dir.close()?;
```

---

# spooled_tempfile in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/fn.spooled_tempfile.html

`pub fn spooled_tempfile(max_size: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [SpooledTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.SpooledTempFile.html) [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)## Expand description

Create a new [ SpooledTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.SpooledTempFile.html). Also see

[.](https://docs.rs/fn.spooled_tempfile_in.html)

`spooled_tempfile_in`[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This variant is secure/reliable in the presence of a pathological temporary file cleaner.

[§](https://docs.rs#backing-storage)Backing Storage

By default, the underlying temporary file will be created in your operating system’s temporary
file directory which is *often* an in-memory filesystem. You may want to consider using
[ spooled_tempfile_in](https://docs.rs/fn.spooled_tempfile_in.html) instead, passing a storage-backed filesystem (e.g.,

`/var/tmp` on
Linux).[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

The temporary file will be automatically removed by the OS when the last handle to it is closed. This doesn’t rely on Rust destructors being run, so will (almost) never fail to clean up the temporary file.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use tempfile::spooled_tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
let mut file = spooled_tempfile(15);
writeln!(file, "short line")?;
assert!(!file.is_rolled());
// as a result of this write call, the size of the data will exceed
// `max_size` (15), so it will be written to a temporary file on disk,
// and the in-memory buffer will be dropped
writeln!(file, "marvin gardens")?;
assert!(file.is_rolled());
```

---

# TempDir in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/struct.TempDir.html

`pub struct TempDir { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A directory in the filesystem that is automatically deleted when it goes out of scope.

The [ TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html) type creates a directory on the file system that
is deleted once it goes out of scope. At construction, the

`TempDir` creates a new directory with a randomly generated name.The default constructor, [ TempDir::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.new), creates directories in
the location returned by

[, but](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir()``TempDir`
can be configured to manage a temporary directory in any location
by constructing with a [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`After creating a `TempDir`, work with the file system by doing
standard [ std::fs](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/index.html) file system operations on its

[, which can be retrieved with](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`[. Once the](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.path)

`TempDir::path()``TempDir`
value is dropped, the directory at the path will be deleted, along
with any files and directories it contains. It is your responsibility
to ensure that no further file system operations are attempted
inside the temporary directory once it has been deleted.[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

Various platform-specific conditions may cause `TempDir` to fail
to delete the underlying directory. It’s important to ensure that
handles (like [ File](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html) and

[) to files inside the directory are dropped before the](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.ReadDir.html)

`ReadDir``TempDir` goes out of scope. The
`TempDir` destructor will silently ignore any errors in deleting
the directory; to instead handle errors call [.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.close)

`TempDir::close()`Note that if the program exits before the `TempDir` destructor is
run, such as via [ std::process::exit()](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/fn.exit.html), by segfaulting, or by
receiving a signal like

`SIGINT`, then the temporary directory
will not be deleted.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary directory with a generated name:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`
let tmp_dir = TempDir::new()?;
```
Create a temporary directory with a prefix in its name:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::Builder;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`,
// whose name will begin with 'example'.
let tmp_dir = Builder::new().prefix("example").tempdir()?;
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Attempts to make a temporary directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.

See [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) for more configuration.

The directory and everything inside it will be automatically deleted
once the returned `TempDir` is destroyed.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`
let tmp_dir = TempDir::new()?;
let file_path = tmp_dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");

writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// `tmp_dir` goes out of scope, the directory as well as
// `tmp_file` will be deleted here.
```
Attempts to make a temporary directory inside of `dir`.
The directory and everything inside it will be automatically
deleted once the returned `TempDir` is destroyed.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use std::fs::{self, File};

writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Attempts to make a temporary directory with the specified prefix inside of
`env::temp_dir()`. The directory and everything inside it will be automatically
deleted once the returned `TempDir` is destroyed.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```

```

`env::temp_dir()`. The directory and everything inside it will be automatically
deleted once the returned `TempDir` is destroyed.

Attempts to make a temporary directory with the specified prefix inside
the specified directory. The directory and everything inside it will be
automatically deleted once the returned `TempDir` is destroyed.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-5)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use std::fs::{self, File};
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of the current directory
let tmp_dir = TempDir::with_prefix_in("foo-", ".")?;

assert!(tmp_name.starts_with("foo-"));
```
Accesses the [ Path](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html) to the temporary directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use tempfile::TempDir;
let tmp_path;
{
   let tmp_dir = TempDir::new()?;
   tmp_path = tmp_dir.path().to_owned();
   // Check that the temp directory actually exists.
   assert!(tmp_path.exists());
   // End of `tmp_dir` scope, directory will be deleted
}
// Temp directory should be deleted by now
assert_eq!(tmp_path.exists(), false);
```
Persist the temporary directory to disk, returning the [ PathBuf](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html) where it is located.

This consumes the [ TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html) without deleting directory on the filesystem, meaning that
the directory will no longer be automatically deleted.

If you want to disable automatic cleanup of the temporary directory in-place, keeping the
`TempDir` as-is, use [ TempDir::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.disable_cleanup) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use std::fs;
use tempfile::TempDir;
let tmp_dir = TempDir::new()?;
// Persist the temporary directory to disk,
// getting the path where it is.
let tmp_path = tmp_dir.keep();
// Delete the temporary directory ourselves.
fs::remove_dir_all(tmp_path)?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/dir/mod.rs.html#429-431)#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/dir/mod.rs.html#429-431)

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Disable cleanup of the temporary directory. If `disable_cleanup` is `true`, the temporary
directory will not be deleted when this `TempDir` is dropped. This method is equivalent to
calling [ Builder::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.disable_cleanup) when creating the

`TempDir`.**NOTE:** this method is primarily useful for testing/debugging. If you want to simply turn
a temporary directory into a non-temporary directory, prefer [ TempDir::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.keep).

Closes and removes the temporary directory, returning a `Result`.

Although `TempDir` removes the directory on drop, in the destructor
any errors are ignored. To detect errors cleaning up the temporary
directory, call `close` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-6)Errors

This function may return a variety of [ std::io::Error](http://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/struct.Error.html)s that result from deleting
the files and directories contained with the temporary directory,
as well as from deleting the temporary directory itself. These errors
may be platform specific.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let tmp_dir = TempDir::new()?;
let file_path = tmp_dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut tmp_file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `tmp_dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(tmp_file);
tmp_dir.close()?;
```

# override_temp_dir in tempfile::env - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html

## Expand description

Override the default temporary directory (defaults to [ std::env::temp_dir](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html)). This function
changes the

*global*default temporary directory for the entire program and should not be called except in exceptional cases where it’s not configured correctly by the platform. Applications should first check if the path returned by

[is acceptable.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`If you’re writing a library and want to control where your temporary files are placed, you
should instead use the `_in` variants of the various temporary file/directory constructors
([ tempdir_in](https://docs.rs/fn.tempdir_in.html),

[, the so-named functions on](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile_in.html)

`tempfile_in`[, etc.).](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`Only the first call to this function will succeed. All further calls will fail with `Err(path)`
where `path` is previously set default temporary directory override.

**NOTE:** This function does not check if the specified directory exists and/or is writable.

# Builder in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/struct.Builder.html

`pub struct Builder<'a, 'b> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Create a new temporary file or directory with custom options.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new `Builder`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a named temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use std::ffi::OsStr;
use tempfile::Builder;
let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-note")
    .suffix(".txt")
    .rand_bytes(5)
    .tempfile()?;
let name = named_tempfile
    .path()
    .file_name().and_then(OsStr::to_str);
if let Some(name) = name {
    assert!(name.starts_with("my-temporary-note"));
    assert!(name.ends_with(".txt"));
    assert_eq!(name.len(), "my-temporary-note.txt".len() + 5);
}
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use std::io::Write;
use std::fs::File;
use std::ffi::OsStr;
use tempfile::Builder;
let dir = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-dir")
    .rand_bytes(5)
    .tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```
Create a temporary directory with a chosen prefix under a chosen folder:

```
use tempfile::Builder;
let dir = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-dir")
    .tempdir_in("folder-with-tempdirs")?;
```
Set a custom filename prefix.

Path separators are legal but not advisable.
Default: `.tmp`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use tempfile::Builder;
let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-note")
    .tempfile()?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#460-463)#### pub fn [permissions](https://docs.rs#method.permissions)(&mut self, permissions: [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html)) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#460-463)

#### pub fn [permissions](https://docs.rs#method.permissions)(&mut self, permissions: [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html)) -> &mut Self

Set the permissions for the new temporary file/directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-notes)Platform Notes

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

This setting is only fully-supported on unix-like platforms. On Windows, if this method is
called with a [ Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html) object where

`permissions.readonly` returns true, creating
temporary files and directories will fail with an error.[§](https://docs.rs#unix)Unix

On unix-like systems, the actual permission bits set on the tempfile or tempdir will be
affected by the `umask` applied by the underlying syscall. The actual permission bits are
calculated via `permissions & !umask`. In other words, depending on your umask, the
permissions of the created file may be more restrictive (but never more permissive) than the
ones you specified.

Permissions default to `0o600` for tempfiles and `0o777` for tempdirs. Note, this doesn’t
include effects of the current `umask`. For example, combined with the standard umask
`0o022`, the defaults yield `0o600` for tempfiles and `0o755` for tempdirs.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasi)WASI

While custom permissions are allowed on WASI, they will be ignored as the platform has no concept of permissions or file modes (or multiple users for that matter).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

Create a named temporary file that is world-readable.

```
use tempfile::Builder;
use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
let all_read_write = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o666);
let tempfile = Builder::new().permissions(all_read_write).tempfile()?;
// Check that this worked and that the file is world-readable.
//
// NOTE: the file likely won't actually be created with 0o666 permissions because it's
// restricted by the user's umask.
//
// NOTE: This test will fail if the user's umask is, e.g., 0o066.
let actual_permissions = tempfile.path().metadata()?.permissions();
assert_eq!(actual_permissions.mode() & 0o044, 0o044);
```
Create a named temporary directory that is restricted to the owner.

```
use tempfile::Builder;
use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
let owner_rwx = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o700);
let tempdir = Builder::new().permissions(owner_rwx).tempdir()?;
let actual_permissions = tempdir.path().metadata()?.permissions();
assert_eq!(
    actual_permissions.mode() & !0o170000,
    0o700,
    "we get the narrow permissions we asked for"
);
```

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self

Disable cleanup of the file/folder to even when the [ NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)/

[goes out of scope. Prefer](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#method.keep)

`NamedTempFile::keep`[where possible;](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.keep)

`TempDir::keep``disable_cleanup` is provided for testing & debugging.By default, the file/folder is automatically cleaned up in the destructor of
[ NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)/

[. When](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir``disable_cleanup` is set to `true`, this behavior is
suppressed. If you wish to disable cleanup after creating a temporary file/directory, call
[or](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#method.disable_cleanup)

`NamedTempFile::disable_cleanup`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#method.disable_cleanup)

`TempDir::disable_cleanup`[§](https://docs.rs#warnings)Warnings

On some platforms (for now, only Windows), temporary files are marked with a special
“temporary file” (`FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY`) attribute. Disabling cleanup *will not* unset
this attribute while calling [ NamedTempFile::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#method.keep) will.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use tempfile::Builder;
let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
    .disable_cleanup(true)
    .tempfile()?;
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#716-721)#### pub fn [make](https://docs.rs#method.make)<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<R>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#716-721)

#### pub fn [make](https://docs.rs#method.make)<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<R>>

Attempts to create a temporary file (or file-like object) using the
provided closure. The closure is passed a temporary file path and
returns an [ std::io::Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html). The path provided to the closure will be
inside of

[. Use](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir()`[to provide a custom temporary directory. If the closure returns one of the following errors, then another randomized file path is tried:](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.make_in)

`Builder::make_in`This can be helpful for taking full control over the file creation, but leaving the temporary file path construction up to the library. This also enables creating a temporary UNIX domain socket, since it is not possible to bind to a socket that already exists.

Note that [ Builder::append](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.append) is ignored when using

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.make)

`Builder::make`[§](https://docs.rs#security-2)Security

This has the same [security implications](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#security) as
[ NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html), but with additional caveats. Specifically, it is up
to the closure to ensure that the file does not exist and that such a
check is

*atomic*. Otherwise, a

[time-of-check to time-of-use bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-of-check_to_time-of-use)could be introduced.

For example, the following is **not** secure:

```
use std::fs::File;
use tempfile::Builder;
// This is NOT secure!
let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| {
    if path.is_file() {
        return Err(std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists.into());
    }
    // Between the check above and the usage below, an attacker could
    // have replaced `path` with another file, which would get truncated
    // by `File::create`.
    File::create(path)
})?;
```
Note that simply using [ std::fs::File::create](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.create) alone is not correct
because it does not fail if the file already exists:

```
use tempfile::Builder;
use std::fs::File;
// This could overwrite an existing file!
let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| File::create(path))?;
```
For creating regular temporary files, use [ Builder::tempfile](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.tempfile) instead
to avoid these problems. This function is meant to enable more exotic
use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking-4)Resource leaking

See [the resource leaking](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html#resource-leaking) docs on `NamedTempFile`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-4)Errors

If the closure returns any error besides
[ std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.AlreadyExists) or

[, then](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.AddrInUse)

`std::io::ErrorKind::AddrInUse``Err` is returned.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use std::os::unix::net::UnixListener;
use tempfile::Builder;
let tempsock = Builder::new().make(|path| UnixListener::bind(path))?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#739-756)#### pub fn [make_in](https://docs.rs#method.make_in)<F, R, P>(&self, dir: P, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<R>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/lib.rs.html#739-756)

#### pub fn [make_in](https://docs.rs#method.make_in)<F, R, P>(&self, dir: P, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedTempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)<R>>

This is the same as [ Builder::make](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.make), except

# tempfile::env - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/env/index.html

Override the default temporary directory (defaults to std::env::temp_dir). This function
changes the global default temporary directory for the entire program and should not be called
except in exceptional cases where it’s not configured correctly by the platform. Applications
should first check if the path returned by env::temp_dir is acceptable.

# TempPath in tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.27.0/tempfile/struct.TempPath.html

`pub struct TempPath { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A path to a named temporary file without an open file handle.

This is useful when the temporary file needs to be used by a child process, for example.

When dropped, the temporary file is deleted unless `disable_cleanup(true)` was called on the
builder that constructed this temporary file and/or was called on either this `TempPath` or the
`NamedTempFile` from which this `TempPath` was constructed.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Close and remove the temporary file.

Use this if you want to detect errors in deleting the file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file cannot be deleted, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Close the file, but keep the path to it around.
let path = file.into_temp_path();
// By closing the `TempPath` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly, the
// file will still be deleted when `file` goes out of scope, but we
// won't know whether deleting the file succeeded.
path.close()?;
```
Persist the temporary file at the target path.

If a file exists at the target path, persist will atomically replace it.
If this method fails, it will return `self` in the resulting
[ PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html).

Note: Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems. Also
neither the file contents nor the containing directory are
synchronized, so the update may not yet have reached the disk when
`persist` returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Only use this method if you’re positive that a temporary file cleaner won’t have deleted your file. Otherwise, you might end up persisting an attacker controlled file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let mut file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let path = file.into_temp_path();
path.persist("./saved_file.txt")?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#256-274)#### pub fn [persist_noclobber](https://docs.rs#method.persist_noclobber)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(
    self,
    new_path: P,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#256-274)

#### pub fn [persist_noclobber](https://docs.rs#method.persist_noclobber)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(
    self,
    new_path: P,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html)>

Persist the temporary file at the target path if and only if no file exists there.

If a file exists at the target path, fail. If this method fails, it will
return `self` in the resulting [ PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html).

Note: Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems. Also Note: This method is not atomic. It can leave the original link to the temporary file behind.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-1)Security

Only use this method if you’re positive that a temporary file cleaner won’t have deleted your file. Otherwise, you might end up persisting an attacker controlled file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location or a file already exists
there, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::Write;
let mut file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let path = file.into_temp_path();
path.persist_noclobber("./saved_file.txt")?;
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/tempfile/file/mod.rs.html#299-315)

#### pub fn [keep](https://docs.rs#method.keep)(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[PathBuf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html), [PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.PathPersistError.html)>

Keep the temporary file from being deleted. This function will turn the temporary file into a non-temporary file without moving it.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

On some platforms (e.g., Windows), we need to mark the file as non-temporary. This operation could fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
let mut file = NamedTempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let path = file.into_temp_path();
let path = path.keep()?;
```

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Disable cleanup of the temporary file. If `disable_cleanup` is `true`, the temporary file
will not be deleted when this `TempPath` is dropped. This method is equivalent to calling
[ Builder::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.disable_cleanup) when creating the original

`NamedTempFile`, which see for
relevant warnings.**NOTE:** this method is primarily useful for testing/debugging. If you want to simply turn
a temporary file-path into a non-temporary file-path, prefer [ TempPath::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.TempPath.html#method.keep).

Create a new TempPath from an existing path. This can be done even if no file exists at the given path.

This is mostly useful for interacting with libraries and external components that provide files to be consumed or expect a path with no existing file to be given.

When passed a relative path, this function first tries to make it absolute (relative to the current directory). If this fails, this function uses the relative path as-is.

**DEPRECATED:** Use [ TempPath::try_from_path](https://docs.rs/struct.TempPath.html#method.try_from_path) instead to handle the case where looking up
the current directory fails.

Create a new TempPath from an existing path. This can be done even if no file exists at the given path.

This is mostly useful for interacting with libraries and external components that provide files to be consumed or expect a path with no existing file to be given.

Relative paths are resolved relative to the current working directory. If the passed path is empty or if the current working directory cannot be determined, this function returns an error.

**NOTE:** this function does not check if the target path exists.

Yields a [ &str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) slice if the

`Path` is valid unicode.This conversion may entail doing a check for UTF-8 validity. Note that validation is performed because non-UTF-8 strings are perfectly valid for some OS.

```

1.0.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/path.rs.html#2553)#### pub fn [is_absolute](https://docs.rs#method.is_absolute)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/path.rs.html#2553)

#### pub fn [is_absolute](https://docs.rs#method.is_absolute)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns `true` if the `Path` is absolute, i.e., if it is independent of
the current directory.

-
On Unix, a path is absolute if it starts with the root, so `is_absolute`and`has_root`
-
On Windows, a path is absolute if it has a prefix and starts with the root: `c:\windows`is absolute, while`c:temp`and`\temp`are not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
assert!(!Path::new("foo.txt").is_absolute());
```
Returns `true` if the `Path` has a root.

-
On Unix, a path has a root if it begins with `/`.
-
On Windows, a path has a root if it: - has no prefix and begins with a separator, e.g., `\windows`
- has a prefix followed by a separator, e.g., `c:\windows`but not`c:windows`
- has any non-disk prefix, e.g., `\\server\share`

- has no prefix and begins with a separator, e.g.,

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
assert!(Path::new("/etc/passwd").has_root());
```
Returns the `Path` without its final component, if there is one.

This means it returns `Some("")` for relative paths with one component.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the path terminates in a root or prefix, or if it’s
the empty string.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
let path = Path::new("/foo/bar");
let parent = path.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Path::new("/foo"));
let grand_parent = parent.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(grand_parent, Path::new("/"));
assert_eq!(grand_parent.parent(), None);
let relative_path = Path::new("foo/bar");
let parent = relative_path.parent();
assert_eq!(parent, Some(Path::new("foo")));
let grand_parent = parent.and_then(Path::parent);
assert_eq!(grand_parent, Some(Path::new("")));
let great_grand_parent = grand_parent.and_then(Path::parent);
assert_eq!(great_grand_parent, None);
```
Produces an iterator over `Path` and its ancestors.

The iterator will yield the `Path` that is returned if the [ parent](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.parent) method is used zero
or more times. If the

[method returns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.parent)

`parent`[, the iterator will do likewise. The iterator will always yield at least one value, namely](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None``Some(&self)`. Next it will yield
`&self.parent()`, `&self.parent().and_then(Path::parent)` and so on.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
let mut ancestors = Path::new("/foo/bar").ancestors();
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("/foo/bar")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("/foo")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("/")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), None);
let mut ancestors = Path::new("../foo/bar").ancestors();
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("../foo/bar")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("../foo")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("..")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Path::new("")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), None);
```
Returns the final component of the `Path`, if there is one.

If the path is a normal file, this is the file name. If it’s the path of a directory, this is the directory name.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the path terminates in

`..`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use std::ffi::OsStr;
assert_eq!(Some(OsStr::new("bin")), Path::new("/usr/bin/").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some(OsStr::new("foo.txt")), Path::new("tmp/foo.txt").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some(OsStr::new("foo.txt")), Path::new("foo.txt/.").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some(OsStr::new("foo.txt")), Path::new("foo.txt/.//").file_name());
assert_eq!(None, Path::new("foo.txt/..").file_name());
assert_eq!(None, Path::new("/").file_name());
```
